title: 'A narcissist': Victim's family hits out at Bryan Kohberger for challenging conviction for Idaho murders
description: The family of one of the victims of Bryan Kohberger has hit out after it emerged that he was challenging his conviction for four murders of students i
body: The family of one of the victims of Bryan Kohberger has hit out after it emerged that he was challenging his conviction for four murders of students in the US state of Idaho.Kohberger was sentenced last year to four consecutive terms of life in prison after pleading guilty to charges of murder in the November 2022 killings.In recent days, Kohberger told the New York Times, external he was taking back his plea, which was made to avoid the death penalty. He said it had rested on "false promises and blatant disinformation".The family of Kaylee Goncalves, one of the students who was killed, said that Kohberger was a "narcissist" who appeared to have changed his position."He chose not to leave his fate - or the facts of the case - to a jury," their statement from the Goncalves family said. "He never cried foul, never claimed he was uninformed or pressured, and never suggested there were problems with the discovery materials he and his counsel had reviewed for two years that should have been challenged."The Goncalves family went on to say "the real tragedy" was the amount of attention that Kohberger was now receiving at the expense of the victims.Kohberger was convicted of stabbing to death housemates Kaylee Goncalves, Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle and Madison Mogen, who all attended the University of Idaho, in their off-campus home on 13 November 2022. The case shocked the small student town of Moscow and made national headlines for almost two months before Kohberger was arrested.Kohberger was a criminology doctorate student at a different institution, Washington State University. He never shared a motive with the court and it is not clear why he would have driven to another campus to brutally stab four students. Investigators were unable to link him to the victims although they presented compelling evidence that put him at the scene of the crime.In his statement to the New York Times, declaring his new intention to enter a not-guilty plea, Kohberger protested his innocence and said he was offering prosecutors another chance to file for the death penalty if they wanted to.Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador paid tribute to the victims' families, saying they had "already endured unimaginable loss and now must face today's deeply painful news".Labrador's statement added: "My office stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out."

schema.headline: 'A narcissist': Victim's family hits out at Bryan Kohberger for challenging conviction for Idaho murders

title: Shots fired at US consulate in Toronto for a second time this year
description: Toronto police said they were investigating the latest attack with the help of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) and international law enforcem
body: Toronto police said they were investigating the latest attack with the help of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) and international law enforcement partners.Supt Jonathan Ko with the RCMP called it "another troubling incident", while the city's mayor, Olivia Chow, called the attack "brazen". "I want to say to the person or persons responsible: We will get you," Chow added.The shooting occurred around 04:45 local time (09:45 BST). Officers said they recovered one shell casing at the scene and damage to the building's facade. At least two individuals were inside the consulate at the time, Toronto Police Deputy Chief Frank Barredo said, but he noted the building is "very heavily fortified" and those inside likely did not hear the gun shot.He added that the investigation remains ongoing and that police across the city have been asked to look out for the potential suspects."We will bring the people responsible to justice," Barredo said.In a post on X, the US consulate in Toronto thanked the police for their response. Police have been stationed outside the consulate since March, when shots were fired outside the building in what police at the time called a "national security incident". No one was injured in that attack. In June, police carried out raids in relation to the shooting. Police officer Marc Pinizzotto, 43, was killed during the operation. Police later arrested several suspects aged 18 and 19 for allegedly carrying out a string of shootings, including the March attack outside the consulate, as part of a larger gun-for-hire network.Two Jewish-owned bakeries in the city were also targeted, at least one by gunfire, over the weekend. Police said on Monday there was currently nothing to link the two incidents, but they did not rule out a connection. "I'm totally disgusted by the shootings and vandalism that took place in Toronto over the last few days," Ontario Premier Doug Ford said.Prime Minister Mark Carney, meanwhile, said he was "appalled" and added: "Law enforcement has my full support as they conduct a thorough investigation and hold those responsible to account."In May, US officials arrested an Iraqi national, 32-year-old Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, for allegedly planning more than a dozen attacks in North America and Europe targeting Jewish institutions and US interests, including the one at the US consulate in Toronto.Police in Toronto have not said if al-Saadi is linked to their investigation, and they have not specified a motive for this latest consulate shooting.

schema.headline: Shots fired at US consulate in Toronto for a second time this year

title: Odyssey translator slams Nolan's film adaptation as 'gimmicky' with 'no sex'
description: Odyssey translator writes scathing review of Nolan film adaptationImage source, Universal PicturesByEmma SaundersCulture reporterUpdated 2 hours agoSi
body: Odyssey translator writes scathing review of Nolan film adaptationImage source, Universal PicturesByEmma SaundersCulture reporterUpdated 2 hours agoSir Christopher Nolan's latest film, The Odyssey, may have won rave reviews from critics and done storming business at the box office - but one person is definitely not happy.Emily Wilson, the academic whose 2017 translation of Homer's Odyssey was cited by the director as an influence on his adaptation of the poem, has written a scathing review of the movie.Published in the London Review of Books, external, Wilson said she "would be ashamed to have written any of this script", describing the film's narrative structure as "gimmicky.""The writing is abysmal," she said. "None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible."Image source, Universal PicturesImage caption, Lupita Nyong'o stars as Helen of Troy in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey"It lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth," Wilson wrote, while also acknowledging that Sir Christopher's work had sparked renewed interest in Homer's classic."The release of The Odyssey is still an event to celebrate," Wilson noted. "This epic is bringing audiences back to cinemas... translations of Odyssey, including mine, are flying off the shelves... [and] perhaps the film will persuade a few college administrators not to cut their literature, language and history departments."Nolan... is doing his best to get the general public reading again, and I am grateful."Image source, Universal PicturesImage caption, The Odyssey is Sir Christopher Nolan's first film since the Oscar-winning OppenheimerBut she was left largely disappointed by the three-hour epic"I had hoped that Nolan's affinity with these Homeric themes might push him to new creative heights, and enable him to conjure more believable characters," she wrote."But The Odyssey features his usual combination of grandiosity and superficiality... the film's vision is too confused, its characters too underdeveloped, to deliver what it half-promises in terms of big ideas – although it is very good at conveying big bangs and big giants."Wilson added that her teenagers had "had a good time" seeing the blockbuster at the cinema."It's a family-friendly audiovisual spectacle, like an elaborate Fourth of July fireworks display - and with about the same level of narrative and emotional depth," she said."There are more female characters than in most Nolan movies, thanks to the source material. But none of them has much to say, in contrast to the characterisations in the poem."During his press tour for the film, Sir Christopher told Empire magazine, external that he used the opening line of Wilson's translation ("Tell me about a complicated man") as a guide for his Odysseus, played by Matt Damon.Image source, Universal PicturesImage caption, Anne Hathaway plays Odysseus's wife Penelope, who's also mother to their son Telemachus (Tom Holland)In contrast to Wilson's take, the latest adaptation has received rapturous reviews from film critics.It is the director's first movie since 2023's Oppenheimer, which won the Academy Award for best picture.The Telegraph declared The Odyssey the "film of the year", while Metro added that the movie would "change cinema forever".The Times described it as "a masterpiece in every way", and the Standard praised the film as a "colossal piece of cinema".The Odyssey, which was released earlier this month, stars Zendaya, Tom Holland, Robert Pattinson, Anne Hathaway, Charlize Theron alongside Nyong'o and Damon.It follows Odysseus (Damon), the Greek king of Ithaca, on his long and perilous journey home from the Trojan War to return to his wife and son (Hathaway and Holland).

schema.headline: Odyssey translator slams Nolan's film adaptation as 'gimmicky' with 'no sex'

title: Wildfires in south-west France flare up as region braces for new 40C heatwave
description: This summer's fourth heatwave was expected to start by Wednesday, bringing temperatures in the area to 40C.Similar temperatures are expected in Spain.
body: This summer's fourth heatwave was expected to start by Wednesday, bringing temperatures in the area to 40C.Similar temperatures are expected in Spain.Dozens of communities are still threatened by wildfires that forced more than 70,000 to evacuate their homes over the last week - although many have now been allowed back.The Madrid region has been especially affected, but Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said while there were highly challenging hours and days ahead, light was beginning to appear "at the end of the tunnel".In neighbouring Portugal, 400 firefighters were tackling a large fire on three active fronts in the eastern Guarda area.The French city of Bordeaux, which has a population of 260,000, is not currently under threat, according to officials, despite the fact that one of the wildfires burning on Monday came only 15km (9 miles) from the city's periphery. But Commander Rémi Lassoureille, who is leading the firefighting response in the Gironde region, is still worried about the western edge of the wildfire."We are frightened about the impact on Bordeaux and the metropolitan area," he said. Air quality in the city also deteriorated greatly."By Sunday evening everything had really begun to empty out," a holidaymaker from Essex told the BBC, adding that the air was "really smoky" with bits of ash. "People were staying indoors, so it was eerie, and very sad."The majority of residents and tourists were wearing masks and the smell of smoke clung on to clothes for days, she said. A firefighter "got a round of applause" as he walked through the Marché des Chartrons in Bordeaux where restaurants were having to close their doors because of the ash in the air, she added."The city has been very quiet," said Graham White, president of the Bordeaux British Community. "The shops, restaurants and cafes are fairly empty... Interestingly on Sunday when there was still smoke, there were people brave enough to sit outside on terraces."White, who has been living in the area for several years, said this sort of event was "something significant". But some news reports had suggested the situation in Bordeaux was "akin to being the next Great Fire of London", which was not the case, White added.Health Minister Stéphanie Rist said the government was being "very vigilant" in terms of air pollution and urged people in the affected areas to stay indoors. On Tuesday morning the Gironde prefect ordered a new evacuation of all camping sites near the coast at Lacanau, while those in the nearby town were allowed to stay put but told to prepare for sudden evacuation. About 4,000 tourists told to leave the area are in addition to the 220,000 people evacuated around France in recent days. An estimated 240 homes and houses have been destroyed, officials have said.By midday on Tuesday firefighters were already intervening in various parts of the region to tackle fires that were picking up again. A 23-year-old man who was arrested on suspicion of starting a fire in the Var region. is now facing 15 years' imprisonment. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that 184 people had been arrested since 6 July in connection with the fires.Peggy Plouhinec, the general director of Château Picque Caillou - one of the few wine estates on the west side of Bordeaux - told the BBC that her business chose to close at the weekend because of the smoke, but that the situation had improved since then and that a bout of rain on Sunday night had helped. While her vineyards were not at risk, she said tourists had "deserted" the region. "The hospitality sector will be impacted this summer, that's for sure," she added. "What is happening is unprecedented. We're lucky that we haven't been too affected yet, but the business will still suffer from the lower numbers of tourists.""But many people have lost their homes or their businesses, not to mention the firefighters who have been hard at work for weeks now and who must be exhausted."One resident of Cap Ferret, which was evacuated late last week, told French media that his main concern now was for the peninsula he lived in, rather than the big city city inland."Everyone talks about saving Bordeaux, but in Bordeaux there's nothing but concrete. Have you ever seen concrete burn?""Here, there are only trees... and when you see all that has burned, it's a catastrophe."Additional reporting by Xavier Pallas

schema.headline: Wildfires in south-west France flare up as region braces for new 40C heatwave

title: US singer D4vd to go on trial for murder in death of Celeste Rivas Hernandez
description: A judge has ruled that US musician D4vd will go on trial for murder over the death of a teenage girl.The decision came after a five-day preliminary he
body: A judge has ruled that US musician D4vd will go on trial for murder over the death of a teenage girl.The decision came after a five-day preliminary hearing, in which Los Angeles prosecutors questioned a dozen witnesses and displayed graphic photographic evidence as 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez's family watched on.The star, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, is accused of killing the girl, whose remains were found last September in a Tesla registered to his address.Burke, 21, has pleaded not guilty to charges of murdering and sexually abusing her.Burke is scheduled to be in court next on 31 August to have the charges against him formally read. The trial is to start within 90 days of that date.The charges include first-degree murder, mutilation of human remains and child sexual abuse. The murder charges include special circumstances linked to financial gain that could make Burke potentially liable for the death sentence.Prosecutors have alleged Burke stabbed the teen before dismembering her body after years of sexual abuse.The accusation of murder ​for financial gain is among the special circumstances included ​in the charges making Burke potentially liable for ⁠the death sentence.They allege he killed her because the teen had threatened to reveal his relationship with a minor and destroy his multi-million dollar music career.Evidence read in court on Monday showed threats Hernandez made to Burke on 22 April 2025, stemming from arguments about his friendship with another girl."I swear to GOD I will kill u", one expletive-laden text said, followed by a threat to strangle him and tell her dad lies about him. "i will end ur career and ur life I will damage anything," the text went on.The following day, Hernandez went to Burke's Hollywood home in an Uber he had sent to pick her up.Prosecutors alleged that Burke stabbed her once she arrived.During questioning at the hearing on Monday, Detective Corey Farrell of the Los Angeles Police Department said text messages indicated that the defendant and the girl had attended church with her family.  In response to the defence, the detective said he was aware the teen had misrepresented her age to the defendant, telling him she was 16 and 18 at different times.Burke's defence lawyers argued there was not sufficient evidence that he had committed the crime.They said her parents were aware of what was going on between them and had even given written consent for her to travel to London with Burke for a week. The defence highlighted texts on the 22nd and the 23rd of April that suggested Celeste had insisted on going to Burke's Hollywood Hills home and that he had argued against her coming before agreeing to send her an Uber on the night of the 23rd.He "repeatedly expressed love and care for Ms Hernandez after they broke up", defence attorney Marilyn Bednarski said in court.The medical examiner's inability to prove how the two penetrating wounds found in the girl occurred and the lack of surveillance video capturing Burke being home on the night of 23 April showed a lack of evidence, the defence argued.

schema.headline: US singer D4vd to go on trial for murder in death of Celeste Rivas Hernandez

title: Number of suspects in fatal Bite of Seattle food festival shooting rises to three
description: Seattle police say they now believe at least three people were involved in a fatal shooting at a food festival on Sunday.Police initially said two sus
body: Seattle police say they now believe at least three people were involved in a fatal shooting at a food festival on Sunday.Police initially said two suspects were thought to have been shooting at each other at the annual Bite of Seattle food festival at the Space Needle - one of the city's most popular tourist spots.However, court papers relating to the arrest of one of these, a 15-year-old, on Monday revealed they now think there is a third attacker. One is still being sought by police, while the other is thought to have been killed at the scene. Three people were killed in the shooting and at least four others were injured, including a two-year old boy. The teenage suspect waived his initial appearance in court on Monday, and he was remanded in custody pending trial, according to local media.Ahead of the hearing, police revealed in court documents that they believe that three suspects may have fired shots during the "gunfight".Court papers filed by the police say investigators are searching for "at least one other unknown suspect", according to local media. Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, speaking at a news conference on Monday, said: "Police continue to look for a third possible suspect."The three people who died on Sunday were 19-year-old Junior Cee Niko Semo, Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba, 44, and Ashley Whitehead, 56, according to the King County medical examiner. Police now believe that Semo was involved in the gunfight.Two deaths were confirmed at the scene, and one person died in hospital.Two guns were recovered at the scene, police said. Speaking on Monday afternoon, Assistant Police Chief Nicole Powell said that preliminary information indicated the shooting may have been "gang-related".She added that the 15-year-old suspect and the 19-year-old who was killed are believed to be "associated with each other". She declined to describe their connection.Sunday was the final day of the annual three-day free food festival, which draws some 350,000 people each year.Videos shared online showed people crouched on the ground, taking cover behind pillars and shelves of merchandise in the Space Needle's lobby during the shooting.Leanne Coles, another witness, told CBS News, the BBC's US partner: "Everybody started running, and so we just ran too, and we ran through the garden and we ducked and we decided to keep running with the crowd."Faith Adia Hunter told the Associated Press news agency that one of the shooters was near her and her friends when they heard the shots, sending them fleeing for shelter in the Seattle Children's Museum."We were right next to him when it started so we took off running," she said. Washington Governor Bob Ferguson said on social media: "My prayers are with the families of the victims, and the responders as they work to keep people safe." Mayor Wilson also condemned the shooting as an "act of horrific violence".

schema.headline: Number of suspects in fatal Bite of Seattle food festival shooting rises to three

title: China's new challenge as natural disasters strike - fake AI videos
description: As China deals with the fallout of Typhoon Noul that made landfall over the weekend, officials will be painfully aware that they will likely have an a
body: As China deals with the fallout of Typhoon Noul that made landfall over the weekend, officials will be painfully aware that they will likely have an additional challenge to deal with: dangerously misleading videos created with Artificial Intelligence (AI).Powerful storms and flooding incidents over the last few months have seen fake videos inundating social media platforms –  these include images of dead bodies floating in floodwaters, the false depiction of severe flooding in areas actually not affected and others with blatantly fake details of emergency response efforts.In some areas, videos containing false information about power outages prompted residents to panic buy emergency supplies.Other videos capitalise on real-life incidents. Flooding in Hengzhou city, Guangxi in early July caused hundreds of snakes to escape from a breeding farm. Then fake images were also published showing crocodiles being released into a river.In an already tense and dangerous situation involving mass evacuations and complex rescue operations, authorities want to avoid panic. Now they fear that AI technology - which China is pouring billions of dollars into - is providing simple, accessible tools that can be used to trick the public."Many of these content creators use disaster news to try to gain followers, knowing that more sensational or exaggerated content will garner more likes and more views. They are deliberately fabricating information to grab people's attention," Huang Zhihua, Deputy Chief in charge of online public security for Zhejiang Police Department told Chinese state media.In recent weeks, there have been arrests and punishment – ranging from detention awaiting criminal prosecution to fines – for the creation of bogus reports and video content.But experts are warning that an unprecedented crisis of misinformation could be looming.In an article published by the newspaper of the Communist Party's Central Party School, Professor Chen Bin said, "AI dramatically lowers the technical barriers to producing false information. Individuals no longer require sophisticated technical skills. By simply prompting AI tools, they can rapidly generate convincing text, images, audio and video… which is highly realistic but entirely fabricated content, manufactured on a large scale."Professor Gao Fuping, from the East China University of Political Science and Law, told the BBC that motivation for the publishing of such false content ranges from those who do it "to create something amusing without thinking about the consequences", to those who want to "generate traffic for personal gain" or those who wish to deliberately "cause panic or social unrest"."Some users think the online world is anonymous and unregulated or that they cannot be traced," he said.There have been calls for all AI-generated content to be clearly stamped but other users can then just re-edit the material removing the markings.Professor Xu Xiaoke from Beijing Normal University told the BBC that greater efforts were also needed to verify geographic locations with timestamps and the checking of image sources."That said, I would also stress that detection technology still lags behind generation technology. We're in a constant cat-and-mouse game. So we should not assume that technology alone can identify AI-generated content with the click of a button," he warned.The Chinese government is embracing AI in its bid to become the leading tech superpower.In 2017,  it announced that AI would be "the main driving force" of the country's progress.Vast sums of money is pouring into AI businesses seeking more capital, fuelling domestic competition. The state-controlled wire service Xinhua reports that the country has over 6,000 "AI companies".In this climate,  Prof Xu believes that China needs to build "trusted information infrastructure". This could include official government early warning systems and disaster interfaces which news organisations can access.But there have been instances of official sources, including government-controlled media, deliberately downplaying disasters, which has led to some public mistrust in this area.Earlier in July, local journalists were asked to "soften" their language to describe a major breach in the wall of the Liulan Dam near Naning as an "opening" or "gap".Officials appeared to be trying to make the breach sound less alarming but the consequences were deadly.  Water bursting through the broken dam led to at least 26 deaths downstream.And this is not an isolated incident.In 2021, local officials were arrested, accused of concealing or underreporting 139 deaths in Henan province.Incidents like these have resulted in a trust vacuum that has made it much easier for bad actors to spread fake content.But police are imploring people to trust accredited sources during emergencies."When encountering disaster-related information from an unknown source, approach it with scepticism and rely on official announcements," Gao Kai from the Ningbo Public Security Bureau said.He also tried to reassure the public that the creators of false information would be caught, saying that "the internet is not a lawless zone. Public security authorities will continue to intensify efforts to crack down on illegal online activity"."We've created a specialised task force to monitor social media closely, especially short video platforms. They will investigate and handle these cases quickly, cracking down in a very strict manner".Punishment could range from a fine to up to seven years in prison if the fallout of the misinformation is serious enough.On 23 July, China's Cyberspace Administration also announced a nationwide crackdown on fake internet content related to floods and other disasters, ordering its local branches to focus on catching out fabricated data, malicious editing, staged scenes, misattributed historical events and those impersonating officials. In addition, it called on social media platforms to strengthen the review of the content they are publishing.Prof Gao believes "the answer is public education combined with law enforcement", saying that there was a "need to publicise real cases where people have been punished."He added that "the harm caused by AI-generated fake content is ultimately the result of how people choose to use the technology - not the technology itself", adding that existing laws were sufficient to deal with it.However, others are not so confident.  Professor Chen pointed out that "AI technology continues to evolve much faster than legal frameworks. As new legal questions emerge, AI misinformation remains a considerable challenge."Shanghai and Washington based lawyer Peter Pang says lawyers around the world are seeing an explosion in the number of cases dealing with these issues.He believes that the companies that create AI apps and the platforms used to publish fake videos and other material must be held legally accountable along with the people who create misinformation."The first line would be the platforms, because they're the ones that are the enablers. They're the ones that allow this to go out," he told the BBC.He used a hypothetical example of a person who runs over a pedestrian following panic induced by a fake post on social media."The video creator might say 'you ran over somebody. That's your problem. I didn't do it.' But let's think it through. You created the foundation from which people reacted. If you created that panic, you need to have responsibility for consequences that occur."And Professor Xu warns that "AI-generated misinformation is likely to increase not only in volume but in the speed with which it spreads.""Looking ahead, political elections, public health emergencies, armed conflicts, natural disasters and issues affecting people's livelihoods are all likely to become high-risk areas for AI-generated misinformation."Instead of waiting for false information to go viral before trying to contain it, governments and platforms should now be preparing in advance."

schema.headline: China's new challenge as natural disasters strike - fake AI videos

title: Chester Zoo staff rescue near-extinct snails from remote rock
description: Zoo conservationists have bred 300 near-extinct tiny snails and introduced them back into the wild.Just 21 Madeiran lands snails were found clinging t
body: Zoo conservationists have bred 300 near-extinct tiny snails and introduced them back into the wild.Just 21 Madeiran lands snails were found clinging to a rock on Portugal's Bugio Island. They were believed to be the last of their kind.Experts at Chester Zoo said they had to brave treacherous conditions and climb cliffs to return them to their natural home, which is part of the Madeira archipelago in the Atlantic ocean.The Madeira government had asked the Chester Zoo experts to help with the snail conservation.The conservationists had scramble from the water up a cliff face in the dark to find cracks in the rocks where the snails could be safely left.Tamas Papp, assistant team manager for invertebrates at Chester Zoo, said: "We knew we had one shot to save them."If we missed this chance, that was it: they were gone."

schema.headline: Chester Zoo staff rescue near-extinct snails from remote rock

title: US walks out of UN Security Council meeting during France's remarks
description: The US delegation walked out of a UN Security Council meeting on Monday, in protest at comments made by France that compared Washington's voting on hu
body: The US delegation walked out of a UN Security Council meeting on Monday, in protest at comments made by France that compared Washington's voting on human rights to that of authoritarian states.The diplomatic row was initially sparked last week, when the US joined North Korea and Russia in voting against extending Volker Turk's term as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. After the vote on Friday, France's UN mission criticised the US and compared it to North Korea and Russia. "The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore," it posted on X, external.In response, US ambassador Mike Waltz accused France of voting for a human rights chief who had been "lecturing" democratic countries while "cozying up to the world's worst oppressors", without elaborating on what he meant.Turk has criticised Russia's war in Ukraine and Israel's military conduct in Gaza.The US team's walkout came while France's ambassador Jerome Bonnafont was speaking during an emergency Security Council meeting on Russia's war in Ukraine.US ambassador Dan Negrea said the delegation would continue to make similar protests until France "renounces their condescending and disrespectful rhetoric".The fight over Turk's second term, which was passed with 144 states in favour, 10 against and 13 abstentions, reflects tensions between Washington and the United Nations.The Trump administration has cut funding for UN agencies and withdrawn from dozens of its entities.On Friday, US ambassador Jeff Bartos criticised Turk's reappointment and said "there will be consequences" to the assembly which "tolerates procedural overreach, backroom deals, and the misuse of UN posts". "The United States will immediately reassess our engagement, participation, and funding," he said.However, French ambassador Bonnafont described Turk as "a voice of conscience" who demonstrated "rigor and impartiality" during his first term.Deputy UN spokesperson Farhan Haq declined to comment on the US walkout, adding the UN expected all member states to respect the decision.

schema.headline: US walks out of UN Security Council meeting during France's remarks

title: Wu Chi-wai: Hong Kong activist allowed to stay in UK after deportation threat
description: Former Hong Kong opposition leader Wu Chi-wai has been allowed to stay in the UK with his family for six months, after initially being detained at the
body: Former Hong Kong opposition leader Wu Chi-wai has been allowed to stay in the UK with his family for six months, after initially being detained at the border.Wu had arrived at London's Heathrow Airport last Wednesday, where he was detained for nearly 10 hours and initially refused entry, he told BBC Chinese. He said he was later told he could stay for only one week, after which he would have to report to the airport to be deported.But on Monday, the UK Border Force approved his entry and granted him a standard stay of six months, he said.The 63-year-old was the leader of the now-defunct Democratic Party and one of the most recognisable faces of the city's quashed pro-democracy movement.Wu is one of the so-called Hong Kong 47, a group of high-profile pro-democracy leaders who were sentenced to jail after a controversial national security trial.He was released in June after spending more than five years in prison for subversion and other convictions.Wu told BBC Chinese that his son and wife moved to the UK in 2022 and 2023, and the only communication he had with them since then was through monthly phone calls and letters. He had hoped to reunite with his family in the UK during his recent visit, he added.Ahead of his departure, Wu said he had consulted staff at the British Consulate General in Hong Kong, asking if there would be any problems with his entry."The information I received was that there would be none," he said, adding that consular staff said they would explain his criminal record and itinerary to the UK Border Force.The Border Force said he was not considered a "genuine visitor" who was solely visiting family, he said.Wu denies that he had intended to apply for political asylum in the UK - a claim that was previously reported in the media.Rights group Hong Kong Watch, which had called on UK authorities to allow Wu to stay in the country, said in a statement that it welcomed the recent news."This is the right outcome, and it should never have taken this long," Megan Khoo, Hong Kong Watch's policy director, said in a statement on Monday. "He should never have faced the prospect of removal back to the city that jailed him."Wu was using his British National (Overseas) (BNO) passport - a special travel document issued to Hong Kong permanent residents before 1 July 1997, when Hong Kong returned to Chinese rule - to enter the UK. BNO passport holders are typically allowed to stay in the UK visa-free for six months.Since 2021, the UK government launched a visa programme for BNO passport holders. Those granted the visa are eligible to work, study and live in the UK, putting them on a pathway to citizenship after they settle in the UK.The new policy came after Hong Kong was rocked by massive pro-democracy protests, which authorities cracked down on. Since then, Hong Kong has come under increasing control from Beijing, and many of its pro-democracy figures have been either fled the city or been jailed.More than 230,000 Hong Kongers have been granted BNO visas and nearly 170,000 have already relocated to the UK, according to the UK government. The UK Home Office, which oversees the UK Border Force, told BBC Chinese on Monday that it does not comment on individual cases, but stated that "the UK government remains steadfast in its support for the Hong Kong community in the UK".A spokesperson from HKSAR Government told BBC Chinese that it has not received any requests for assistance from Hong Kong residents to date.

schema.headline: Wu Chi-wai: Hong Kong activist allowed to stay in UK after deportation threat

title: French Navy carries out 'shooting drill' in English Channel mid BBC interview
description: Figure caption, A French Navy boat was heard firing shots during a BBC interview earlierByDaniel SextonSouth EastUpdated 1 hour agoA French Navy patro
body: Figure caption, A French Navy boat was heard firing shots during a BBC interview earlierByDaniel SextonSouth EastUpdated 1 hour agoA French Navy patrol boat appeared to fire a round of gunshots "without warning" in the English Channel during a BBC interview with the UK shadow home secretary.Conservative MP Chris Philp was being interviewed about small boat crossings by BBC journalist Michael Keohan as a French warship passed by at 09:15 BST (10:15 CET), about three miles from the French coast.Keohan said there were 17 shots but "no warnings" from the boat about 300m away, which left Philp believing it was an intimidation tactic to "stop us covering migrant crossings".The French authorities said it was part of a training exercise, unrelated to the presence of a British ship, which it said was out of range of fire.Philp dismissed this claim as "not credible", adding: "There were no warnings in place about live firing training exercises."It looked and sounded exactly like deliberate intimidation."Image source, BBC/Jack ValpyImage caption, Chris Philp MP, the Shadow Home Secretary, said it felt like an intimidation tactic or warning shotsThe captain of the fishing boat which hosted the interview, Matt Coker, said he had "never seen anything like it before".The French authorities said the boat, PSP Flamant, was not engaged in an operation to monitor migrant boats.Keohan said there were 17 shots, adding: "There was no warning for our boat, no signs given that this was the French's intention."Philp said it "felt to me like an attempted intimidation to stop us covering migrant crossings".Image source, Richard Pohle/The TimesImage caption, A French patrol officer at the back of the boat was seen pointing a pistol towards the seaAt sea, Keohan described it as "the most unusual moment... in the quiet of the Channel" when the gunshots rang out mid-interview.A French patrol officer at the back of the boat was seen pointing a pistol towards the sea. It is believed that is where the shots came from.Keohan, who was on board the vessel with a reporter from The Times, added: "There was no warning for our boat, no signs given, that this was the French's intention. "Even now it's still not clear what the patrol boat was aiming at."Image source, Chris Philp MPImage caption, The MP was being interviewed by the BBC at the time of the incidentAfter the incident, Philp said: "It is extraordinary that the French Navy will fire live rounds to defend their waters against a visiting British politician but cannot bear to do anything about stopping illegal Channel crossings."If France showed people smugglers half the seriousness they showed me, the boats would stop. "Instead, the French wave them through and pass them off to the British coastguard so it's our problem."He said he would be raising the issue with the French ambassador.'Normal activity'A UK government spokesperson said: "This is a matter for the French authorities."The French authorities said a handgun shooting exercise had taken place by the public service patrol boat Flamant off the coast of Cap de Gris-Nez.A spokesperson said: "In order to maintain their high level of operability in the current international context, the units of the French Navy train regularly."Individual training of the combatant is part of the normal activity of a ship in operations."The regulatory signals as provided for by international standards for this shooting exercise were displayed, and the safety gauge was respected."This exercise is unrelated to the presence of a British ship in the area, which was out of range of fire."The PSP Flamant was not engaged in an operation to monitor migrant boats."Earlier this month, a Russian warship, shadowed by a Royal Navy vessel, carried out a live-fire artillery exercise just 46 miles (74km) south of Plymouth.Follow BBC Kent on Facebook, external, on X, external, on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

title: World Cup: Uefa furious at reports Fifa plan to sell stakes in tournament
description: European football's governing body Uefa has reacted furiously to proposals from Fifa to seek private investment in its competitions, including the Wor
body: European football's governing body Uefa has reacted furiously to proposals from Fifa to seek private investment in its competitions, including the World Cup.Fifa - the sport's global governing body - said it intends to expand "football development funding" to more than $10bn (£7.5bn) and invite third-party investment in a new venture.The story was first reported in the Financial Times and the Times, with the latter claiming the plans could potentially earn Fifa president Gianni Infantino tens of millions of pounds.In a lengthy statement outlining the proposals, Fifa says it will " invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) - to "consolidate" its commercial and event operations.Fifa say that once approval has been granted, Thrive Eternal is expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.Fifa sources have told BBC Sport there has been no discussion over Infantino, or anyone else, becoming chief executive of the new body.In its statement, Fifa did say Infantino and the rest of the organisation "has a duty" to control the development of the project.Fifa has not said precisely what that means, or what the specific nature of Infantino's involvement will be.As part of its pitch Fifa says all member associations will be able to access up to $20m (£15m) in "one-off capital" to fund development.Infantino said every nation should benefit from the riches football creates."Parts of the game have turned that popularity into remarkable commercial value - and we celebrate that success and want it to continue, because it lifts the whole game," he said."Our job is to make sure the rest of football grows with it: Fifa exists to support sustainable, inclusive development in every corner of the world."However, Uefa has issued a statement criticising the proposals, which it claimed "crosses a line".Fifa argues its plan, with a dedicated commercial subsidiary, is similar to that used by governing bodies in other sports.In 2018, Premiership Rugby announced a partnership with private equity and investment advisory firm CVC Capital Partners.However, Uefa sees Tuesday's announcement as a step too far - and raises the potential for further expansion of Fifa competitions in order to raise revenue, both in terms of size and frequency, which could threaten its own lucrative competitions."This crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross," Uefa said."Uefa takes it extremely seriously. So should every National Football Association. So should every stakeholder who cares about the future of the game."The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade - especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not Fifa's to sell."Fifa says it would retain control of FFE "and exclusive authority over football governance, competitions, the international match calendar and all regulatory and sporting decisions".The matter is likely to be a topic of conversation at the next Fifa Council meeting in the autumn and then around the Fifa Intercontinental Cup, featuring Champions League winners Paris St-Germain, in December.The proposal could be voted on by all 211 members at the Fifa Congress in Morocco in March.

title: Japan earthquake: What we know so far
description: Figure caption, ByGeorge WrightUpdated 4 minutes agoJapan is reeling from the latest major earthquake to hit the country.Nineteen people are missing a
body: Figure caption, ByGeorge WrightUpdated 4 minutes agoJapan is reeling from the latest major earthquake to hit the country.Nineteen people are missing at an Aeon shopping centre and a paper factory after the 6.8 magnitude earthquake hit Kyushu island, an official said.The quake has also caused power cuts, damaged roads, collapsed a castle wall and destroyed a footbridge.Information is still coming out of Japan but here is what we know so far.When and where in Japan was the earthquake?The quake hit the Kumamoto prefecture on Kyushu island at 16:27 local time (07:27 GMT) on Tuesday, with hundreds of thousands of people being told to move to evacuation shelters.The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) reported the earthquake had a magnitude of 7.1, which the US Geological Survey later measured as a 6.8. Quake magnitude figures are often updated as seismologists obtain and analyse new data.Kumamoto - where the collapsed Aeon Mall is located - is a city on the Kyushu island of Japan.The southern island of Kyushu is the third-largest of the four main islands in Japan, and the second most populous.The Kumamoto prefecture is no stranger to earthquakes.A total of 278 people were killed in 2016 by powerful quakes in Kumamoto and neighbouring Oita prefectures, according to Japan's public broadcaster NHK.Image caption, A map of the epicentre of the earthquake in Kumamoto prefecture on Kyushu islandPeople remain trapped inside an Aeon Mall in Kumamoto prefecture, the fire service said.Ten people remain unaccounted for at the shopping centre, an official at the Disaster Management Division of Kumamoto prefecture told the BBC.Four people have been rescued from the mall and their lives are "not in danger", the official added.A witness reported seeing an explosion and smoke at the shopping mall after the quake.The witness saw the second floor of the building collapse, with some shoppers taken to hospital.Japan's fire and disaster management agency later confirmed that the second floor of a "commercial facility" collapsed, with many people trapped inside.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Kumamoto - where the collapsed Aeon Mall is located - is a city on the Kyushu island of JapanWhere else has been affected?Elsewhere in the Kumamoto prefecture, a chimney reportedly collapsed at Nippon Paper's Yatsushiro Plant, according to police, who are being cited by NHK.An aerial photograph of the site obtained by Reuters news agency appears to show a broken and collapsed chimney.The disaster management official told the BBC that two people at the plant had been found in a state of "cardiac arrest" and nine people are still missing.Image source, ReutersImage caption, People are thought to be missing after a chimney collapsed at the Nippon Paper Industries Yatsushiro PlantTremors also caused historic walls at the 17th-century Kumamoto castle to tumble.It is not the first time the castle has succumbed to an earthquake. When a 7.3 magnitude quake hit the region in 2016, parts of the 400-year-old castle were also damaged as turrets and curved walls collapsed.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Tremors damaged walls at the 17th-century Kumamoto castleA footbridge also collapsed in the Kumamoto region.It is unclear if anyone was injured, or when the collapse took place. Traffic appears to be travelling on the bridge that runs parallel to it.More than 40,000 households are without power, according to an update on Kyushu Electric's website. There has also been damage to roads.There have been more than 60 aftershocks ranging in magnitude from 1 to 4, Japan's Meteorological Agency said.A tsunami warning was issued immediately after the quake, ​but was lifted within two hours.

title: 'It's a hell of a situation': Spain grapples with major wildfires
description: Temperatures are expected to approach 40C in some regions in the coming days, with the heatwave forecast to last at least until Sunday.Spain's state m
body: Temperatures are expected to approach 40C in some regions in the coming days, with the heatwave forecast to last at least until Sunday.Spain's state meteorological agency Aemet has warned the "fire danger level will continue to rise to extreme levels, hindering firefighting efforts".Regional authorities began lifting some evacuation and lockdown orders on Tuesday as conditions improved - including in parts of the Madrid region - but restrictions remain in place in the worst-affected areas.In the Madrid region alone, more than 56,500 people have been evacuated since the fires broke out last week. A further 27,797 people have been ordered to stay at home. Further evacuations have taken place in Ávila, Toledo and Valencia.Ayuso had earlier described the wildfires as "the biggest natural catastrophe in the history of Spain".She wrote on X that the situation was now "improving little by little" and some residents may soon be allowed to return home.Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told Spain's La 1 TV channel that firefighting efforts on Monday night had resulted in "relatively positive progress"."This morning, we are very satisfied with the work done. We are going to consolidate the work that has been done," he said.He maintained that "we must be positive; we have the emergency under control" but conceded that "weather conditions are not helping us at all".Spanish journalist Juan Navarro, who is in Cebreros - a town around 40 miles west of Madrid – told the BBC that people were looking with fear to the next heatwave.When you drive through villages in the area around Cebreros, "everything is black", he said.The mayors of two of the evacuated towns in the Madrid region described the fire as "a kitten by night and a lion by day".Robledo de Chavela mayor Fernando Casado said his community would continue fighting "with their knives out".Echoing his sentiments, Valdemaqueda mayor Ricardo Meneses added that "we can't let our guard down and we're on high alert because now is the time to stop the fire".A psychologist visiting shelters has told El Mundo there is a growing sense of anxiety among the evacuees."We've seen cases of people who come in relatively relaxed on the first day because they think this situation might only last a day," said Sara Casado, of the Citizen Services Department of the Madrid region."But then they see how the hours and days go by. That uncertainty of being here without knowing when they'll be able to return increases their anxiety."The Madrid region is currently under a red weather warning, with temperatures expected to reach 35C in mountainous areas and 38C in other parts of the community.In its latest update, the national government's delegation in Madrid said the fire "remains active and uncontrolled"."Today's efforts will focus on surveillance and cooling the affected areas in anticipation of the forecast worsening of weather conditions," it added.Around 77,000 hectares (190,000 acres) have been affected by the fires in Spain, according to the minister for ecological transition, Sara Aagesen.The wildfire burning in the Ávila area was the largest in the country's recent history, she added.In Ávila, where more than 50,000 hectares have burned down since the start of the wildfires, the government's representative said the fire had a "quite favourable" evolution overnight.Nicanor Sen, however, said there had been "small flare-ups" that were now being monitored by emergency services.Meanwhile, the government of Valencia lifted a lockdown order for the town of Vall D'Uixo after a fire broke out of 25 July, forcing some 16,000 from 20 municipalities to evacuate.However, the local council's fire department representative, David Vicente, told the press on Tuesday afternoon that the fire remains "very active".In neighbouring Portugal, firefighters are tackling a large fire on three active fronts in the eastern Guarda area. The Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere (Ipma) has put large parts of the country under a very high red fire alert, with some areas under the highest warning level.

schema.headline: 'It's a hell of a situation': Spain grapples with major wildfires

title: Roberto Mancini next Italy manager after Andrea Pirlo controversy
description: Pep Guardiola and Carlo Ancelotti were both approached by the FIGC about the Italy job before Pirlo.Mancini, 61, previously managed Italy from 2018 un
body: Pep Guardiola and Carlo Ancelotti were both approached by the FIGC about the Italy job before Pirlo.Mancini, 61, previously managed Italy from 2018 until 2023 and won Euro 2020 - beating England in the final at Wembley.He led the Azzurri to a world record 37-game unbeaten run, but failed to qualify for the 2022 World Cup - losing to North Macedonia in a play-off - and resigned in August 2023.Another World Cup play-off failure for Italy earlier this year meant they were absent from this summer's tournament and spelled the end of Gattuso's tenure, with his contract terminated in April by mutual consent.Despite their big stage successes, Italy have not featured at a World Cup finals since 2014.Under-21 manager Silvio Baldini had taken over on a temporary basis following Gattuso's departure.Former Italy and Sampdoria midfielder Mancini led Manchester City to their first Premier League title in 2012 and enjoyed success with Lazio and Inter Milan, winning the Coppa Italia with both and three Serie A titles with Inter.He also spent time with Galatasaray and Zenit St Petersburg before taking on the Italy job in 2018.After he departed from the Azzurri, he had a short spell with the Saudi Arabia national team before joining Qatari side Al Sadd.Although they won the Qatar Stars League, they failed to reach the final four of the AFC Champions League Elite and lost in the Qatar Cup final. Mancini left his role with Al Sadd in June.Italy start their Nations League campaign on 25 September at home to Belgium before travelling to face Turkey three days later.
